A daily pill to fight breast cancer? Swiss firm’s new drug completes 3 phases of human trials

Giredestrant is designed to target breast cancer tumours that are hormone receptor-positive, meaning their growth is driven by hormones such as estrogen.

Akanksha Mishra

21 October, 2026 07:47 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Representational image | Photo: roche.com

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Swiss healthcare company F Hoffmann-La Roche AG is seeking US approval for a new breast cancer pill, giredestrant, which it expects could generate up to $15 billion in revenue, according to a Bloomberg report . The drug has completed three phases of human trials, and the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is expected to decide on its approval by late November or early December.

Giredestrant is a once-daily pill designed to block and degrade estrogen receptors, which can fuel the growth of certain breast cancers. The FDA has granted the drug priority review, expediting the approval process.

Results from a global Phase III trial of the drug were published in the New England Journal of Medicine on 1 October. The study included 373 women and men with hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer whose disease had progressed or returned after treatment.

Show Full Article

The findings showed that patients who took giredestrant after surgery had a lower risk of cancer recurrence than those who received standard hormone therapy. The drug was also better tolerated, with fewer patients discontinuing treatment because of adverse effects.

Giredestrant is designed to target breast cancer tumours that are hormone receptor-positive, meaning their growth is driven by hormones such as estrogen. It belongs to a class of drugs known as selective estrogen receptor degraders (SERDs), which includes fulvestrant and elacestrant, developed by AstraZeneca and Menarini Group, respectively.

A separate study found that giredestrant could also help control advanced breast cancer, prompting Roche to seek a further FDA approval. In patients whose cancer had spread and stopped responding to initial treatments, combining giredestrant with everolimus, a targeted drug, nearly doubled the time they lived without their tumours growing.

According to Bloomberg, the drug could mark Roche’s return to the forefront of breast cancer treatment more than two decades after the launch of Herceptin, its targeted therapy for HER2-positive breast cancer. Herceptin helped establish Roche as a leader in the field, but the company has since faced competition from other drugmakers, including AstraZeneca, which developed Enhertu to treat HER2-positive cancers.

While awaiting the FDA’s decision, Roche is projecting sales potential of up to $15 billion for giredestrant, according to Bloomberg. The company has said the drug is more tolerable than other SERDs, potentially improving patients’ quality of life.

(Edited by Prashant Dixit)

Vivek Ramaswamy doubles down on controversial ad targeting Amy Acton despite backlash

The ad backed by Vivek Ramaswamy features Amy Acton’s estranged mother, who calls her own daughter a liar and accuses her of causing mental health issues.

Manisha Mondal

21 October, 2026 07:17 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Businessman Vivek Ramaswamy makes a campaign visit to Machine Shed Restaurant before the Iowa caucus vote in Urbandale, Iowa, U.S. January 15, 2024 | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Vivek Ramaswamy, Republican nominee for governor of Ohio, has taken responsibility for an ad attacking opponent Democrat Amy Acton.

In the ad, Acton’s estranged mother calls her a “liar” , claiming the Democrat candidate has caused her mental health issues.

Ramaswamy’s team on Tuesday confirmed that they will spend around four million dollars to promote the ad, even if it is facing criticism.

Show Full Article

Acton on Tuesday, in an interview with Spectrum News , said that this has been a “lifelong pattern” of Ramaswamy.

Amy Acton’s childhood  The Democratic candidate Acton has publicly spoken up about her and her brother Stearns facing abuse in their childhood while living with their mother, Donna Arthur.

Acton was three years old when her parents got divorced. The custody of the siblings went to her mother. They changed 18 houses during the first 12 years. They were subjected to poverty and hunger as kids; even Arthur left the siblings with relatives to earn money.

Acton’s stepfather sexually abused and molested her between the ages of 9 and 12. In 1978, Acton’s biological father reported the conduct to authorities, resulting in the arrest of her stepfather. Acton continued to suffer so that she could protect her brother.

Arthur chose to stand by her husband.

Acton’s team published a statement through her brother Phillip Stearns before Ramaswamy’s double down.

“Such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother’s husband into a political talking point,” he said.

Stearns, in his video message, said that their mother “stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died.”

Acton and her brother’s life stabilised after they moved in with their biological father.

“This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core– a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants,” Stearns said in the video.

Also read: Elon Musk says SpaceX-Tesla merger would be a ‘good idea’. Committees formed to explore deal

Ramaswamy’s acknowledgement Since the video started circulating, it drew criticism from Democrats and a few Republicans, The Hill reported.

In a statement given to Associated Press , Ramaswamy’s team said that Acton’s mother was not paid for the one-minute spot.

The promotional ad will continue to air both online and on television as the election nears.

Acton, in her interview, said that she would not let anyone “normalise” her childhood trauma.

“Normalize somebody who has said that my childhood is something I am just complaining about. Who today just released an ad using my birth mother, whom I was removed from at the age of 12 for severe abuse, neglect and sexual abuse,” she said.

Ramaswamy has previously attacked Nikki Haley’s daughter during the 2023 presidential election while both were fighting from the Republican Party.

Casey Putsch, a Republican competing for Ohio Governor elections, wrote that he is voting for Acton.

“In light of the most recent attack by Vivek (by way of manipulating Amy’s family) I have considered this—Vivek and his friends cover up human and child trafficking while attacking Amy Acton over the abuse she endured as a child. These revolting and manipulative men show no care or genuine concern for people or Ohio and that is the reason I was called to run against Vivek in the primary,” he posted on X.

“Amy, may you lead Ohio with compassion for everybody and our future as normal people together”.

(Edited by Ratan Priya)

Global media on India-US ties amid Rubio visit as Trump pauses sanctions on Russian oil

Youth-led SIR protests infuse fresh blood into the Oppn; & risks of judging India against a manufacturing model like China built under different global conditions, international media discusses.

Prakhar Agrawal

21 October, 2026 06:10 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Featured image: Manya Aggarwal

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Today’s international media coverage looks at India through the lens of its ties with Washington, democratic tensions and its future in global supply chains.

Marco Rubio’s visit to India is as much about business as diplomacy. What Mujib Mashal for the New York Times describes as “commercial diplomacy”. In its report , “Rubio Travels to India to Strengthen Economic Ties Amid Strained US Relations”, the New York Times describes a visit aimed at strengthening commercial ties even as President Donald Trump’s tariffs, immigration policies and outreach to Pakistan have strained relations with New Delhi.

Rubio met his counterpart S. Jaishankar in Mumbai and was expected to meet executives from Indian companies with significant US operations, including two of Asia’s richest men, Gautam Adani and Mukesh Ambani.

Show Full Article

Washington is also pushing India to reduce its reliance on Russian oil and source more energy from the US, as negotiations over a bilateral trade deal continue.

Adani, a “close ally” of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, was indicted in the US in 2024 on bribery and fraud charges, which were dismissed in August after he offered to invest billions of dollars on American soil, the NYT reports.

Trump in the past has also announced that Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries will partner in building an oil refinery in Brownsville, Texas. Rubio is visiting Jamnagar, home to Reliance and the world’s largest oil refinery complex. He is also touring Vantara, the wildlife rescue centre built by the Ambani family. Asked whether he would encourage Reliance to resume production in Venezuela, Rubio said: “We’re going to go see what their holdup is and what opportunities exist.”

The visit comes as US-India ties are travelling a bumpy path over tariffs and India’s purchase of Russian oil. Rubio, “who is widely seen as a contender in the next US presidential election,” said New Delhi had made “substantial progress” in reducing those purchases. Yet Washington has itself shifted course, announcing a deal to purchase diesel from Russia. The report highlights the gap between diplomatic engagement and unresolved disagreements.

Ahead of Rubio’s trip, Trump appeared to offer India a concession. On Friday, he paused sanctions related to Russian oil sales, easing pressure on New Delhi as the war in Iran disrupted energy supplies and raised concerns over global oil markets. In “Rubio visits India seeking relief from global energy crunch”, The Wall Street Journal examines how the energy crisis has complicated an already strained relationship between Washington and New Delhi.

The sanctions pause was a “great relief” to Modi’s government, said Sadanand Dhume, a fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. Had the sanctions gone ahead, Dhume said, it would have been a “body blow to the relationship” and seen as “humiliating the prime minister” by making him appear “more or less powerless”.

A trade deal between the two countries also remains unresolved. US ambassador Sergio Gor said last week that the “big items are done”. Despite the tensions, bilateral trade reached a record $240 billion in 2025, and the two countries maintain strong military ties.

But analysts cited by the WSJ say the visit has yet to address many of the underlying disagreements between Washington and New Delhi. As South Asia analyst Michael Kugelman put it, the earlier effort to signal Washington’s appreciation for India had not addressed New Delhi’s concerns over tariffs and US relations with Pakistan. “You can’t solve those policy differences,” he said, “with mere PR”.

That is how Yamini Aiyar opens her New York Times guest essay, “Indian Democracy Has Found New Life in the Streets” , arguing that youth-led protests over voter roll revisions have brought fresh energy to a political opposition struggling to challenge Narendra Modi in the election arena.

Aiyar, a public policy scholar and visiting professor at Brown University, describes how demonstrations led by the Cockroach Janta Party have drawn students, civil society activists and opposition politicians into a common movement.

More than 130 million names have been cut from voter rolls, according to the essay, while critics argue that the process places an unfair burden on citizens to prove their eligibility. Aiyar writes that even minor differences in the spelling of names across documents can leave voters off the rolls, with restoration requiring them to navigate a difficult appeals process. The government denies allegations that the exercise is intended to exclude minorities or groups less likely to support the BJP.

Aiyar describes the moment as “both sobering and thrilling”. After more than a decade of democratic backsliding under Prime Minister Narendra Modi, she writes, institutions across India have been so “hollowed out that public trust” in the electoral process and the Election Commission is crumbling, “while brutal state repression is all too common”. India’s democratic tradition, she argues, placed the responsibility on the state to enroll eligible citizens. The current revision reverses that principle by asking voters to prove they belong, she adds.

Her closing line captures the stakes: “But when the process itself is suspect, each victory means less.”

Apple’s growing business in India has revived a familiar question: Can the country become “the next China”? In an opinion piece, Global Times writer Hu Weijia argues that the comparison may be the wrong scale to measure India’s manufacturing ambitions.

The article quotes The Economic Times as saying that Apple’s India business surpassed Rs 1 trillion, or $10.5 billion, in fiscal 2026. Yet some international commentators remain sceptical that the expansion of iPhone production will transform India into a manufacturing powerhouse on China’s scale. Hu cites Bloomberg opinion columnist Andy Mukherjee’s argument that Apple’s iPhone factories will not make India the next China, but says the debate risks judging India against a manufacturing model built under very different global conditions.

“It is like a train gathering speed but still falling short of its destination,” Hu writes. “Perhaps the problem lies not with the train, but with the destination itself.”

The piece argues that India does not need to reproduce China’s industrial development to benefit from Apple’s expansion. Indian factories are moving beyond basic assembly into more complicated stages of production, while links with established international suppliers could help local manufacturers lower costs and build capacity.

Rather than trying to recreate China’s vast manufacturing ecosystem from scratch, Hu argues, India could benefit from integrating more deeply into global supply chains and drawing on existing industrial expertise.

The argument is also a reminder of Global Times’ own framing: India’s manufacturing success, it suggests, should be measured by the capabilities it develops and the role it secures in global production not simply by whether it can become another China.

(Edited by Viny Mishra)

Elon Musk says SpaceX-Tesla merger would be a ‘good idea’. Committees formed to explore deal

SpaceX is valued at $2 trillion and Tesla at $1.5 trillion. A merger would create one of the largest corporate combinations in history.

Purvi Rajpuria

21 October, 2026 04:13 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

| X: Elon Musk

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Elon Musk on Tuesday said that a merger between his two biggest companies, SpaceX and Tesla, would be a “good idea.”

While the tech billionaire warned that it would be premature to assume the certainty of the merger, he confirmed that special committees had been formed within both companies to examine the move.

Musk has suggested the possibility of a merger between the two companies in the past as well, citing growing overlap between their operations. Last week, British bank Barclays also floated the suggestion that a merger could be announced before Tesla’s annual meeting in December.

Show Full Article

Stock prices for both companies went up after the comment. While shares of SpaceX rose 8 per cent, Tesla’s shares rose 1.8 per cent. The space tech company had also posted its first profit as a public company in the third quarter of this year.

Tesla, an electric car company, is valued at roughly $1.5 trillion. SpaceX, which manufactures space rockets and Starlink internet satellites, is valued at $2 trillion. A combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history.

‘Merit in combining the companies’ Musk recently launched Terafab, a combined effort to manufacture computer chips between SpaceX and Tesla. Additionally, SpaceX acquired X and xAI earlier this year, before it went public. Both these moves point to Musk’s attempts at consolidating his companies, signalling that he sees them as operating more effectively when working together.

A full merger between SpaceX and Tesla would make sense considering both companies do work around chips, artificial intelligence, software and more, the BBC reported .

“I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starlink constellation, connectivity,” Musk said.

The merger, however, would ultimately be decided by shareholders. At least 50 per cent of Tesla’s shareholders would need to approve the merger—something Musk has described as “quite a high hurdle to achieve”.

Also read: Ali G is outdated—and that’s why he’s back, writes Sacha Baron Cohen in TIME

Benefits of the merger? With Musk owning just under half of SpaceX and nearly a fifth of Tesla, analysts have said that a merger would give him control of the combined entity, Reuters reported .

Justus Parmar, Chief Executive Officer at Fortuna Investments, pointed to another benefit of bringing SpaceX and Tesla together in one place, for investors to back.

“Tesla runs a high-margin, cash-generative automotive business and there’s more growth to come with the robotaxis on the way. That cash flow could help support SpaceX’s bottom line and fund its very capital-intensive space exploration and launch goals, including orbital data centers,” he said .

(Edited by Ratan Priya)
